title: Three in the Morning
text:
A man who kept monkeys fed them chestnuts every day. When food grew short, he went to the monkeys and announced a new arrangement: from now on they would get three chestnuts in the morning and four in the evening.

The monkeys were furious. They screamed and jumped about in protest.

So the keeper changed the offer. All right, he said, you can have four in the morning and three in the evening.

The monkeys were delighted and calmed down at once.

Nothing real had changed. They were getting seven chestnuts a day either way. But their anger had turned to joy simply because the same amount was presented in a different order. The keeper had gone along with what the monkeys wanted, and it cost him nothing.

Zhuangzi uses the story to make a point about argument. People wear themselves out insisting that things must be one way, without seeing that the matter is the same underneath. The wise person, he says, lets disputes rest in balance, accepts the monkeys' view where it does no harm, and walks two roads at once.
lesson: People react to how a deal is framed, not only to what it contains. When the substance is the same, letting the other side choose the framing can settle a fight at no cost.
source: Zhuangzi, Chapter 2 (Discussion on Making All Things Equal)
caveat: A version of the same story also appears in the Liezi, where the keeper is a man of Song.
